Therefore, Witness, once again, the word "Mujahidi" and "Mujahedin," in the sense of the Mujahedin Detachment, is not the same, is it?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: No, it's not the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Can we please show page 2 of the document now. In the English, this is also the next page. Page 5 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please focus on this portion of the document which is just above the list of names. It is clear that this report is on its way; you agree, right? And the report is about Mujahidi, the fighters. And then look at the paragraph just above the names. It reads: "The Bosnian Army also took part in this operation under the command of the El Mujahedin Detachment." And then it goes on to say: "Victory, victims," and then a list of victims or casualties. And do you agree -- well, please have a look.

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that in actual fact, the person who wrote this report makes a clear distinction when describing the Mujahidi, the fighters on the one hand, and the El Mujahedin Detachment, on the other hand, which is the very first reference to it in this report?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: Yes, that seems to be the clear inference, based on this letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back once more to the previous page, Your Honours, please, in both the English and the Bosnian. Again have a look. This is a general description of the course of the battle. The Mujahidi, the fighters, are advancing. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would that be your conclusion? This portion is not specifically about the El Mujahedin Detachment, is it?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: That's right. This could be in reference to any other army unit or, indeed, any other fighters who were involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 2 of this document, you just read what the author says. The Bosnian Army was involved under the Command of the detachment. It is clear that whoever asked this report --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the question. May counsel please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Whoever authored this report, when he wrote that the El Mujahedin Detachment -- that in the action the BH Army was involved under the command of the detachment, therefore it is clear that, therefore, the author of the report did not believe that the army was in command of this action; right?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: That is correct. The units that took part in the area of responsibility of the 35th Division, their members were all under the command of the El Mujahedin Detachment in that operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And not the other way around, then?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: That's right, not the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For a minute, can we go back to this report, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Once again, did the El Mujahedin Detachment capture those 61 prisoners? Would you accept that this was proof that these were arrested or captured by the El Mujahedin, that the prisoners of war were captured by El Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: Regardless of what it says in this report and what it specifically refers to, the detachment absolutely did not arrest or capture more than six detainees in that operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said "15", not "six."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said "not more." Can you come close to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And when you say "the detachment," do you mean the El Mujahedin Detachment that captured 15?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. Whenever I say "detachment," I mean the El Mujahedin Detachment. Next time, I will try not to leave out "El Mujahedin."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, Witness, the Prosecutor -- now I'm going to move to something -- something else. I just want to ask you, before that, about this, what you have just said last, please. That day, outside the El Mujahedin Detachment, there were many Arabs who were fighting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: That is correct. I met a group of some 30 of them, and I heard that the whole of Buzuber's [as interpreted] group was present in the field, allegedly over 200 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify for the transcript, you're talking about Abu Zubeir's group? The witness is talking about Abu Zubeir's group. Did you ever have information about those prisoners of war before you -- that this event actually did take place before you spoke with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: Just like I already said in my statement, I had heard about a report that I believe the 2nd Battalion of the 328th Brigade sent requesting that they be paid compensation, funds for the prisoners. At that time, there was a practice that units were rewarded for captured or killed members of enemy forces and also for the capture of equipment, materiel and the like.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's just clarify that. Did anyone from the Bosnian Army Army, or on behalf of the army, or members of the army, asked around the members of the detachment, of those -- for those prisoners? Did the detachment capture prisoners?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: At the time, nobody was asking anything about some group of some 60 detainees, not in that time period during those days or later.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at least not to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: I don't know about it, but I would have to know if something like that happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested is: How did you find out about that report of the 328th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: I heard -- I didn't see that statement, but -- that report, but I did see them asking for that compensation. Well, that was a little bit funny or cute, as far as we were concerned, but we didn't really take that seriously.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't take it seriously because you did not have information that this capture had taken place?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: Well, that capture did not take place.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It did not take place on the part of the El Mujahedin Detachment, at least; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Especially what did not happen was that these prisoners were seized from some other unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. The Prosecutor showed you a document, MFI 832, that had to do with the issuance of permission to go abroad, and in relation to that I would like to ask you: It's correct, isn't it, that the detachment, El Mujahedin itself, had arranged and paid for that; that is correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That was completely arranged by the El Mujahedin Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we can move into closed session once again, and I apologise again. Perhaps this sentence can be redacted from the transcript, because it can also be used to identify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May lines 15 and 16 of page 57 be redacted, please, and may the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: PW-9, can you just briefly clarify for us the relationship between the Emir of the El Mujahedin Detachment and its military commander, in terms of their responsibilities and duties and functions?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: The Commander of the El Mujahedin Detachment, Abu Maali, was responsible for the whole detachment and for everything that happened in the detachment. This implies both his Assistant for military affairs and his other assistants, such as assistants for the Press Centre of the detachment, for religious instruction of the detachment, for the motorised unit, the servicing, everything that was a part of the El Mujahedin Detachment. The deputy -- or assistant commander for military affairs was responsible for the units in the front, for preparation of operations, for military training, for procurement of equipment and materiel that had to do with the army, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And, sir, when you refer to the assistant commander for military affairs, to whom are you referring?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: I am thinking of Muatez Al Masri, who stayed at that function until he was killed on the 22nd of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: PW-9, in your written statement, there are a number of paragraphs that talk about various meetings that you attended with Muatez and with other senior commanders of ABiH units. Do you remember those meetings that you've discussed in your statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, and I remember the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you recall, sir, approximately how many such meetings you personally attended that were attended also by Muatez and senior ABiH commanders?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: There were between seven to ten meetings, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And, sir, what was the time period of these seven to ten meetings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. I think it will be prudent to redact line 25 of page 63, maybe that whole answer. May we then move into private session also.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: PW-9, I now want to turn now to a different topic. I believe earlier this morning, in response to a question by my colleague Madam Vidovic, you told us that there were no more than 15 prisoners of war taken by the detachment during the course of the war. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: No, you didn't. The 15 prisoners were just in the last operation performed by the El Mujahedin Detachment on the 10th of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, when you say -- okay, you've clarified that. Let me ask you this, sir, because in paragraph 256 of your statement, you make reference to around 25 POWs had been taken, and I'm wondering if you recall that and if you can tell us which operation you were referring to in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: I remember that. That was the overall number of prisoners that we took in the Vozuca theatre of war. In the first operation, there were no prisoners. In the second and third, a total of about 25 prisoners were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I think I just have one last topic that I would like to cover with you, and my learned colleague was discussing this with you immediately before the last break. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you told us, sir, as reflected on lines 15 to 23 of page 58 -- I think we do need to go into private session, Your Honours. I think this was covered in private session, so I would ask that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Witness, I wanted to ask you to tell us something about Dzemat. You've talked to us about this. First of all, I would like you to tell me, if I understood you correctly, that the Dzemat was linked to the El Mujahed Detachment and that the Mujahedin from other groups were not part of that group, other Arabs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: If your question is about other Arabs who were involved in the fighting in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in that case what you say is accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. Thank you very much. So regarding all the members of the El Mujahedin Detachment, were they all part of the Dzemat?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more thing. Did you know, personally, each member of the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: No, not each of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And one more question regarding passports and the problems. When it came to issuing passports, when El Mujahedin had to go to a foreign country for medical treatment, do you know, how were they able to come into Bosnia and Herzegovina without having obtained previously a permit to leave the country? Was there a procedure, for instance, for these people to be able to come back after obtaining -- after having had their medical treatment? What was the procedure in place for them to come back?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: There was no procedure. Those people were citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They spent some time abroad and then they returned. I'm not quite certain -- or perhaps you may have misunderstood what I was saying earlier on. I'm not really sure what your question is about, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So then let me clarify before I put the next question to you. Is it only that citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina that were part of the army went to a foreign country for medical treatment or would other members also go to a foreign country for medical treatment, combatants who were foreigners within the detachment?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: I don't know about members of any of the other army units. As for the El Mujahedin Detachment, both the ethnic Bosnians and the foreigners who were part of the detachment went abroad for treatment. Once they had been treated, they, as a rule, returned to the detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So foreigners, how were they able to come back to Bosnia if they would leave Bosnia without a prior authorisation or permit? Was there a procedure in place for these people to come back or was there a procedure through which they had to go before they leave Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no procedure to leave or to return. They required no special approval to return because, in the first place, they required no special approval to leave. As foreigners, they were no military conscripts in Bosnia itself. And you have to keep in mind the fact that Bosnia at the time was not such an organised state as to keep track of all of these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So borders of Bosnia were open during the war and they were open to all foreigners?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were open after the signing of the Washington Agreement, open to all foreigners. I do not know of any restrictions that were placed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And how about before the Washington Agreement; were there any restrictions?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: Prior to the Washington Agreement, for the most part, the BH Army forces, or should I say the forces loyal to the Sarajevo government, were not in control of the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another thing. You talked to us about a separate department that would have functioned -- and of course I will ask you to clarify this, if I understood you correctly, so therefore within the detachment there was a department to greet the newly arrivals, the Arabs who would come, and you called it "The Command of the Arabs," the Arabs' Command. Would you be able to clarify this for us, please? What exactly were you referring to when you mentioned this department or service?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: That's right. Within the detachment itself, there was a special section for admission of foreigners. At first, Abu Muaz Kuwaiti headed that section. They also called him the Emir of the Arabs. Whenever a fresh foreigner turned up in the detachment, this section would interview the person, they would take his personal documents, they would run certain checks and pass him along to be trained for service in the El Mujahedin Detachment, whenever that was needed, and so on and so forth. So between this section and the Personnel Section of the Corps, there was absolutely no link, no exchange of information or documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I would like you to tell us something else about the special section for admission of foreigners. You talked to us about the structure, but this special section, is that the section that Madam Vidovic was referring to when she was talking to -- of a sort of a security organ of the detachment?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: No, that's not the same organ. The security organ was a different organ within the El Mujahedin Detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So unfortunately I need to put one more question to you. Since we've heard in this trial that the detachment did not have its own security organ, this type of security organ, what is it exactly? Could you please clarify this for us?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: I said that this was the Security Service. The Security Service was responsible for the security of the Vatrostalna barracks, as well as the discipline of Bosniaks in the El Mujahedin Detachment. The service was headed by Ezher Beganovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this Security Service was to contact war prisoners; was that part of their function?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: The responsibility for the prisoners of war lay with Muatez, as assistant commander for military affairs, and whoever he personally entrusted to carry -- as to who he personally entrusted to carry out interviews with the prisoners of war is something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. PW-9, I also have some questions for you in relation to your testimonies over these past days. If we just stick to the issue which was raised most recently by Judge Lattanzi about the registration of incoming new foreigners to your detachment, my question is: Do you know how these individuals came to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: From what I understood and learned in conversations with some who did come, their arrival was privately arranged without any particular organisation involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Are you talking about a local Bosnian organisation or organisations in their homelands?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: I don't think there was any organisation by the El Mujahedin Detachment, and I'm not aware that any other organisation got them together and sent them to Bosnia in an organised fashion or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I see. But it couldn't be a coincidence that suddenly a whole number of fighters from Arab countries and other countries would suddenly turn up in Bosnia to assist their Muslim brothers in the war. I mean, there must have been some sort of organisation, some sort of coordination of all of this. Do you know, from your friends in the El Mujahedin Detachment, whether they were invited by the leadership of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or were they offered by other organisations in the Middle East or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: You must know that not all Arabs came to Bosnia together. They would come from the beginning of the war, from 1992, continuously until the end of 1995. For the most part, they would come individually or in small groups of two, three, or five persons. I'm aware that the Arabs were encouraged to come and help in Bosnia, just like this was in the Milano Institute, whose director and found was Sheik Enver El Saban, but I'm not aware that anybody sent persons to Bosnia in an organised fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking, of course, is that for any state, including the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there are national interests associated with foreigners coming into the territory, and so my question to you is if you know that these people who came to assist in the war effort came with the understanding or upon the invitation of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: Today, we talked about the farewell ceremony of the El Mujahedin Detachment, and I recollect that at that ceremony, Abu Maali briefly said why the Mujahids came to Bosnia. If my recollection serves me well, he said they came having seen, thinking of the media, images of the suffering of the Muslim people in Bosnia. I think that was their main motivation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Just to conclude this point, I want to be sure that I have understood you correctly, in that to your knowledge, there was no official involvement of the Government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the entrance into the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina of fighters from abroad; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: I'm quite sure that they were absolutely not included in this or involved in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I have a series of questions relating to the issue of the - what shall I call it - the cooperation or coordination between the El Mujahedin Detachment and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Let me begin this series of questions by referring to the, what should I say, the unfortunate speech which we heard on the television clip -- on the video clip, sorry, where General Delic, if indeed it was him, and I leave that open, but the suggestion that was made was that the El Mujahedin Detachment was -- and I think the words came "was always a part of the army in Bosnia and Herzegovina." That was the quotation that I noted. Now, regardless of whether this speech was authentic or not, I would like you to give me your opinion of exactly that issue. Was the El Mujahedin Detachment a part of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: We saw here the order instructing the formation of the El Mujahedin Detachment on the 13th of August, 1993, and that would, de jure, mean that the detachment was an integral part of the army. However, the El Mujahedin Detachment never functioned like other units that were part of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I've already spoken a number of times about the relationship of the detachment command towards let's call them "superior command," regardless of whether or we're talking about division, operative group, or corps commands. There are also some other indications that could point to this. For example, members of the El Mujahedin Detachment never wore insignia of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The El Mujahedin Detachment never had any flags flying of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in any of its barracks. Ranking officers, whom we also mentioned during my testimony, never actually wore their rank insignia, which was contrary to army regulations. So it can be said that the detachment was de facto another army or a different army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, that is the very core of this trial. Now, just to revert you to your observation that the El Mujahedin Detachment never bore insignia and never flew any of the flags and so on, I have noticed that as well, but I also saw on one of the documents, I think on the first day of your testimony, that a stamp was applied by the El Mujahid Detachment, and I think you referred yourself to the El Mujahid Detachment being a unit, and a four-digit number, I can't remember the digits, but that seemed to me to be a formal indication of the El Mujahid Detachment being a part of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: Yes, that is so. Formally, the detachment was an integral part of the army. We've already said that in relation to the order on the formation of the El Mujahedin Detachment. The stamp had to be used for documents that, in particular, had to do with the Bosnian members of the El Mujahedin Detachment and the resolution of their status as members of the army. None of us or of the detachment command wanted the Bosnian members of the detachment, as military conscript did not want them to be left off the register of Bosnian Army members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: In your statement, paragraph 32, and I would ask the Registrar to assist us in bringing up paragraph 32 of the statement, if possible --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I don't think it is necessary with private session. No, it's not, so you can just go ahead. It's not necessary. My question relates to the same aspect of the relations between the two armed forces here. You say, in paragraph 32, that the El Mujahedin Detachment was a part of the ABiH and it was subordinated to the 3rd Corps. You can read for yourself when you find it.

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: Yes, I said that, and it says in my statement that this was formally that way. Formally, in our language, you could interpret as meaning de jure, but in essence it operated quite differently from the way that a unit should operate in relation to its superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, PW-9, thank you very much, but we are looking to find out what were, then, these differences, and what was the importance or the implications of these differences when it comes to the responsibility for crimes possibly committed during the armed operations?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: I can say with certainty that there were no crimes and that this is superfluous, but it's up to the Court to establish what the essence of these events was. I apologise. Let me just say that there were no crimes on the part of the members of the El Mujahedin Detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, that question is for this Trial Chamber to determine. But let us just for the example, I'm not saying that there were crimes committed or that there were not crimes committed, leave this question aside, but answer me to my question of: Who would be responsible if, hypothetically, a war crime was committed by someone who was a member of the El Mujahid Detachment? This is, of course, a question which has a very legal bearing, and so if you cannot answer it, then please do not try to answer it. It's only if you know, through your position in the El Mujahid Detachment, that perhaps you had discussed these things in advance and that you had an answer ready to the question. But if you don't know, then please do not try to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: First of all, the perpetrator, himself, would be responsible, then his immediate superior in the El Mujahedin Detachment, then Muatez as the military commander, and then --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the name --

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: As the Commander of the El Mujahedin Detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, the interpreter didn't hear the last part of your sentence. "Then Muatez as the military commander," and then?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: And ultimately Abu Maali as the Commander of the El Mujahedin Detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And how would the El Mujahid Detachment deal with these responsibilities? Would the Shura decide or would you -- I mean, how? What would the procedure be for dealing with the commission of war crimes?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: For such a serious matter, probably the Shura would deal with it, would discuss it. As to what would happen, that is something that I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Suppose the hypothetical crime of which we are now talking turned out to be committed by a Bosniak, that is to say, someone who was also a citizen of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, would that person be tried before a Bosnian court or a military court in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: As a member of the detachment, first the Shura would decide his fate, what they would do, would they hand him over further for trial, or whether they would, themselves, deal with the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: PW-9, I realise that this is highly speculative, so unless you are certain about your answers, then don't make those answers. I would rather you would say then that you don't know if you don't know. But you raised the issue of handing over a Bosniak for trial before a Bosnian court, being military or civil court, and we have assumed, just for the example, that the perpetrator was a Bosniak and not a foreigner, just to make the example easier. And I understood you to say that the Shura would then decide whether they would prosecute him on their own or hand him over for trial before a civil or a military Bosnian court. My question to you is: Would this, in fact, be an option, I mean the handing him over to prosecution before Bosnian institutions?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: At the time, I believe that the chances for that would be slight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I don't think we should pursue this matter any further, but I thank you for your answers to this line of questions. Let me then move on to a third line of questions that I had in relation to your testimony, and that concerns the prisoners of war. If I heard you correctly, you said that altogether, during your time in service for the El Mujahedin Detachment, some 25 prisoners of war were seized, and 15 of them were seized at the last operation, the Vozuca operation. My question to you, in relation to these prisoners of war that were taken by the El Mujahedin Detachment, is: What did you do with them?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: These prisoners were handed over to the Military Police of the 3rd Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did the El Mujahid Detachment have a detention facility where they would be able to keep prisoners for shorter or longer times?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: I'm aware that the prisoners were kept or held briefly in the camp of the El Mujahedin Detachment 13 kilometres away. That's where they were interviewed. I don't know who did the interviewing, but I know some information that was received from the interviews with those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: PW-9, I realise that the time has gone, so I will defer to the President for his decision as to what we do now. I must say I do have more questions to put to you, so -- but I'll defer to the President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. We would like you to spend your weekend at home, and for that reason I would like to ask if it is possible, given the fact that the court is available after lunch, can we sit this afternoon to finish this witness? Everybody's nodding. I would like to see in the dark window there if everybody is also nodding there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It seems as if Judge Lattanzi would not be able to, but we can sit 15 bis if it's agreeable by the rest of the people. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm advised that the interpreters might perhaps need to check before they can answer, and I see one head is nodding from the interpreters. And the suggestion is that maybe we could start at 3.00, 3.00 to 4.30. Maybe in one session, we should be able to do it, and that will give the interpreters an opportunity to check, and maybe they can advise the Registrar if they're available and we can sit at 3.00. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We need to check, Your Honours, because in that case we might need to have a new team of interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And then once you have checked, you can then advise the Registrar, who will tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Based on that hope, we'll break, take a break, and come back at 3.00. Thank you. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you to the interpreters for accommodating us. Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. PW-9, we were in the series of questions relating to the prisoners of war, and you told us that at the Kamenica 13-kilometre camp, there was limited detention facilities to keep prisoners there for a short period of time, and you also told us that some of the prisoners were actually held there for some time and that they were questioned by some of the officers of the El Mujahid Detachment. PW-9, did you ever visit the Kamenica camp, and did you see the detention facilities for yourself?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: I went there many times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And did you see the detention?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Were there any prisoners kept in the detention when you went to see it?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: I was there once when there was some prisoners there as well. They had just been taken for a bath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you recall when that was and how many prisoners there were?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: That was after the second operation that the detachment performed. Late July. There were about ten prisoners there, give or take a prisoner or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Were you able to determine their state of health, just superficially, I mean? I know that you're not a doctor, but did they look to you to be in good health?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: They looked all right. They were all able to walk unassisted to the place where they were given a bath. There was no one who was being carried on a stretcher or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You told us that they were interviewed by officers of the -- or members of the El Mujahid Detachment. Do you know if the information gathered by the El Mujahid Detachment was shared with the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: I don't know if this was shared with the 3rd Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know if the ICRC, the International Committee of the Red Cross, was given access to the area?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: No, they had no access. I wasn't aware of any requests that the Red Cross had made to come and visit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And these prisoners, you told us they were then handed over to the Zenica Prison. Do you know how that was arranged and after how long the time of detention?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: At the time, I saw documents listing the names of the prisoners and the signatures of the military police members who took over, as well as the signatures of those who had handed over the soldiers. However, the hand-over procedure itself was not something that I witnessed, and I'm not familiar with any details of the hand-over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know if the 3rd Corps ever made any requests to the El Mujahid Detachment to get access to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to my next series of questions, which relate to your knowledge of the other foreign group of fighters -- groups of fighters in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And after that, Witness, I only have a few questions relating to the Geneva Conventions, but let's first look at your knowledge of the other groups of foreign fighters. You have left us with the impression that you had absolutely no contact with them, you did not coordinate any combat actions with them, you didn't know how many there were, but since you have introduced to us the concept of the Dzemat, my question would be if, at the level of the Dzemat, there would be some sort of contact or exchange of information or coordination between the El Mujahid Detachment and the other groups of foreign fighters in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: I was not aware of any contacts like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you happen to know how these other groups were - how should I say - were arranging their presence in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the government authorities or with the Army of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: I don't know how they came to Bosnia. I don't think they were really interested in resolving any of their own issues with the authorities, the government bodies of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to elicit from them information about how they had arranged their presence in Bosnia and Herzegovina? The information that I'm looking for, if you have it, is whether you knew or heard that they had arranged their presence on more or less the same terms as the El Mujahid Detachment had arranged its existence in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Were they -- in other words, were they there on the same terms as the El Mujahid Detachment? Do you know? If you don't, then just tell us that you don't.

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. My last series of questions goes to the compliance with the rules -- with the international rules of the laws of the war, and I'm curious to know if the members of the El Mujahid Detachment were informed about the Geneva Conventions and, if so, if they were required to comply with the norms of the Geneva Conventions during their combat operations.

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: Members of the detachment were not informed about the Geneva Conventions. They had orders from their superior, Muatez, to the effect that no one was to touch the prisoners. The prisoners were, under no conditions, to be touched or killed. In the actual unit where the prisoners were being held, there were guards around the clock and no one was allowed access to the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If the Geneva Conventions were not being suggested to the members of the El Mujahid Detachment during combat operations as norms governing the hostilities, then what other norms would apply to the El Mujahid members when in combat? What I'm asking about is, of course, the Geneva Conventions do not only relate to prisoners of war, they also have a number of rules governing combat, and my question is: If the rules in the Geneva Conventions did not apply because they were not imposed on the members, then what other rules applied, or were there any rules?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: I must say I'm not privy with the detail of the Geneva Conventions and the rules that stem from the Conventions. As for the rules that the members of the El Mujahedin Detachment complied with, those were rules that they were taught during their training at the El Mujahedin Detachment Training Centre, as well as instructions they received from their superiors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And can you give us an outline of what those other rules were; for instance, relating to killing of enemies during combat?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: As I pointed out in my statement, the El Mujahedin Detachment had such rules that the most important thing was the objective of an operation itself, taking certain features or taking them back from the enemy. The objective of an operation was neither to kill nor to capture an enemy soldier. What happened during operations, of course, was the fact of the battle. Many enemy soldiers were killed. There were no special rules governing that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You also told us about the decapitation or beheading of enemy soldiers. I think you told us that that would have happened after they had been killed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What was the purpose of this? Why would you decapitate a killed enemy soldier and display his head among the civilian populations?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: The purpose in those situations was certainly not to display these heads to the civilians there. They happened to see them simply because they lived in the same villages where members of the El Mujahedin Detachment were staying too. The purpose of the act of beheading itself was to additionally intimidate the enemy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, sir, you told us that at least in two instances, dead enemy soldiers were decapitated on the battlefield and their heads were brought to the village of Livade to be shown to the civilian population there.

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: I don't know how I phrased that. I didn't mean to say that they were displayed to the civilian population. Those people who were living there just saw the heads. They were civilians living there. There were also members of the El Mujahedin Detachment staying in homes in those villages. It's not that these heads were deliberately displayed to the civilians living there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. If I may just ask a few questions. Are you able to tell what the total number of soldiers there were in the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: From the day I joined, the number was on a steady increase. Towards the end of the war, the El Mujahedin Detachment numbered about 1.000 members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know about what number they numbered when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: At the time, there were about 70 members, between 70 and 80 probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Today, in your testimony, you mentioned - or it may be yesterday, I'm not quite sure - that there were various groups of Afro-Asian origin who were fighting in this war. My question is: On whose side were they fighting? Do you know or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: They were fighting on the same side as the El Mujahedin Detachment, the side of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, you just correct me. Did you say to me, sometime during today, that you did not know all the members of the El Mujahedin Detachment, personally?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: That's true, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it possible that you could make a mistake, in terms of your knowledge of the membership of the El Mujahedin Detachment? And I'm suggesting that you could either mistake some of the people who belong to other groups to be members or vice versa?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: Such a thing perhaps could have happened in a town or village out in the street, but certainly not at a time when a combat operation was unfolding. If I may just clarify, the reason was we wore special bands to distinguish us during the actual combat operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How did the armbands look like?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: Those were armbands or ribbons in two or three different colours, depending on the operation. There was always a combination of colours that was used to distinguish members of the detachment from members of all the other units, especially to distinguish us from the enemy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just want to make sure I don't repeat questions that have already been asked by other Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thanks for that clarification. What I do want to find out from you is that: You said, I think on more than one occasion, that you did not know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm advised that we need to go into private session. May we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, how much longer are you going to be, just to double-check with the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have only ten more minutes. I will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please -- witness, that means that until 1994, it was not possible for a single foreigner to enter Bosnia and Herzegovina who had not been let through either by the Croatian or the Serbian authorities, if we leave aside UNPROFOR planes, which is how you got there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And those UNPROFOR flights were something that the Government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had no influence over; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: Yes, they didn't have any influence over those flights.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the Washington Agreement, so just a part of the border was again held by the forces of Bosnian Croats and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Still, the bulk of the border was blocked by Serb forces; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: That is correct. Just the southwestern borders, the borders between Western Herzegovina and the Dalmatian hinderlands were under the control of the Bosnian Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So foreigners who had their own passports were able to go in and out without the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina having any information about that? I'm thinking of the regular authorities of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: PW-9 [Realtime transcript read in error
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And if I may add, the time after the signing of the Washington Agreement was the time when the bulk of foreign nationals joined the detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just like to ask you something else briefly. In response to His Honour Judge Harhoff, in your response and then also elaborating on an answer given to the Prosecution, you spoke about decisions relating to participation in attacks and also meetings that had to do with that. You described -- you said -- Your Honours, if we can now go into closed session for a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now that we are in open session, can I openly say to you thank you very much for accommodating us, all of you, and also thank you to the parties for agreeing to sit this afternoon. This brings us to the conclusion of your testimony today, sir. Thank you so much for coming to testify. You are now excused and you may go -- you may stand down, and we wish you well in your travel back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I beg your pardon. May we please move into private session so the witness may go out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
